title: BEFORE LUKE WROTE A SINGLE WORD, OTHERS HAD ALREADY TOLD THE STORY OF JESUS. SO WHY DID HE WRITE ANOTHER?
paragraphs: BEFORE LUKE WROTE A SINGLE WORD, OTHERS HAD ALREADY TOLD THE STORY OF JESUS. SO WHY DID HE WRITE ANOTHER?

Luke 1:1–4 reveals something extraordinary about the Gospel: Christianity was not built on a rumor that nobody could investigate. It was proclaimed through witnesses, carefully preserved testimony, and a message so important that one physician refused to leave his reader uncertain.
What if I told you that one of the most fascinating statements in the entire New Testament appears before Luke even begins telling us about the birth of Jesus?
Before the angels appeared to shepherds.
Before Mary laid her newborn Son in a manger.
Before Jesus healed the sick, forgave sinners, confronted religious hypocrisy, or walked toward the cross.
Luke quietly revealed something that many Christians have read a hundred times without realizing how significant it is.
Other people had already written accounts about Jesus.
Not one.
Not necessarily two.
Many.
And Luke knew it.
He didn't hide it. He didn't pretend he was the first person to document the extraordinary events surrounding Jesus Christ.
Instead, he opened his Gospel by acknowledging the accounts that came before him.
That raises an uncomfortable question for anyone who has ever wondered whether the Bible can be trusted.
If many accounts already existed, why did Luke need to write another one?
Were the earlier accounts incomplete?
Were people telling different stories?
Was Luke trying to correct someone?
Or was something far more remarkable happening beneath these four verses?
Because when we examine what Luke actually wrote in Greek, rather than what we sometimes assume he meant, we discover an author who was remarkably open about his sources, his method, and his purpose.
And somewhere in that discovery is a message for the person who believes in Jesus but sometimes lies awake wondering whether their faith can survive difficult questions.
Luke was not afraid of questions.
He was writing so that someone could have greater certainty.
Listen carefully to his opening words.
"Forasmuch as many have taken in hand to set forth in order a declaration of those things which are most surely believed among us,
Even as they delivered them unto us, which from the beginning were eyewitnesses, and ministers of the word;
It seemed good to me also, having had perfect understanding of all things from the very first, to write unto thee in order, most excellent Theophilus,
That thou mightest know the certainty of those things, wherein thou hast been instructed."
— Luke 1:1–4, King James Version
At first glance, it sounds like a formal introduction.
Almost administrative.
But look closer.
Luke is telling us how he approached writing about the most consequential life in human history.
And he begins with one Greek word that deserves our attention.
Ἐπειδήπερ — Epeidēper.
It means something like "inasmuch as" or "since indeed."
This is not the language of someone suddenly experiencing a private vision and rushing to record it.
Luke is introducing a reasoned explanation.
He is preparing his reader to understand why this account exists.
Then comes the phrase that has puzzled generations of readers:
πολλοὶ ἐπεχείρησαν — polloi epecheirēsan.
"Many have undertaken."
The word polloi means "many."
The verb epecheirēsan means "undertook" or "attempted."
But here's where we need to be careful.
Some people see the word "attempted" and assume Luke was criticizing earlier writers for failing.
That is not what the Greek necessarily means.
The verb can simply describe undertaking a task. Luke does not explicitly accuse those earlier writers of dishonesty, incompetence, or theological error.
He acknowledges that others had already undertaken the work of composing narratives.
That distinction matters.
Because Scripture deserves better than dramatic claims its words cannot support.
And faith does not become stronger when we exaggerate what the Bible says.
Luke's next words make the picture even clearer.
He says these writers undertook to compile a διήγησιν — diēgēsin, a narrative or account.
Of what?
Of events that had taken place among them.
The Greek phrase is:
τῶν πεπληροφορημένων ἐν ἡμῖν πραγμάτων
A close rendering is "the matters that have been fulfilled among us."
The word peplērophorēmenōn comes from a verb that can communicate fulfillment or full assurance, depending on context.
That is why English translations differ.
The King James Version says "most surely believed among us."
Many modern translations render the phrase along the lines of "things that have been fulfilled among us."
In Luke's broader Gospel, fulfillment is an important theme. God's promises are coming to their appointed realization in Jesus Christ.
But we should not pretend that the Greek has no interpretive difficulty. Responsible translation recognizes both the wording and the context.
Luke is not merely saying, "Here are some interesting religious opinions."
He is writing about events that he and the Christian community understood as profoundly significant in God's unfolding work.
And this leads to something even more important.
Luke did not ask his reader to believe that the story began with him.
He pointed backward.
Toward witnesses.
Toward testimony.
Toward people who had been there.
He writes:
καθὼς παρέδοσαν ἡμῖν οἱ ἀπ᾽ ἀρχῆς αὐτόπται
"Just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses handed them down to us."
That word autoptai means eyewitnesses.
People who saw.
People who were present for the events they reported.
Luke also calls them servants or ministers of the word.
And the verb paredosan, meaning "handed down" or "delivered," is significant.
It describes the transmission of testimony.
Christianity did not emerge in Luke's Gospel as a disconnected collection of inspirational sayings.
Luke places his narrative within a chain of witnesses and communicated teaching.
But we must also acknowledge something important.
Luke does not claim in these verses that he personally witnessed every event he describes.
He distinguishes the eyewitnesses from those, including himself, who received their testimony.
That is not a weakness he tries to conceal.
It is part of his stated method.
And there is something refreshingly honest about that.
Imagine someone writing about an event today and openly explaining that they had consulted earlier accounts, received testimony, and investigated the material before preparing their own narrative.
Would we automatically call that person unreliable?
Of course not.
We would want to examine their sources, their methods, and their conclusions.
And that is precisely the kind of serious engagement Luke's introduction invites.
But there is another question.
Who were these earlier writers?
We don't know all their names.
Luke does not identify them.
He does not give us a list of documents.
He does not say exactly how many narratives existed or which ones he personally used.
Scholars commonly understand the Gospel of Mark as one important source behind Luke's Gospel, and many scholars believe Luke also drew on other written and oral traditions.
The precise relationships among Matthew, Mark, and Luke remain subjects of scholarly discussion.
What we cannot responsibly say is that Luke 1:1–4 proves he possessed every Gospel we have today.
Nor can we say that all the earlier accounts were false, lost, suppressed, or rejected.
Those claims go beyond what the passage tells us.
What Luke does tell us is remarkable enough.
He knew that accounts existed.
He knew that testimony had been transmitted.
And he believed there was value in writing his own carefully prepared narrative.
Why?
Because of a man named Theophilus.
Luke addresses him as:
κράτιστε Θεόφιλε — kratiste Theophile.
"Most excellent Theophilus."
The name Theophilus means "lover of God" or "friend of God."
Some have suggested that the name was symbolic, representing anyone who loves God.
That is an interesting possibility.
But the formal address "most excellent" also appears elsewhere in Acts for officials of high standing, such as Felix and Festus.
So many interpreters understand Theophilus as a real individual, possibly a person of social standing.
We cannot identify him with certainty.
But we can identify Luke's stated concern for him.
Theophilus had already received instruction.
He was not being introduced to Christianity from nothing.
And yet Luke wanted him to know the certainty of what he had been taught.
Read that again.
He had already been taught, but Luke still wanted him to be certain.
That sentence may speak to someone reading this right now.
Maybe you grew up in church.
You know the songs.
You can finish the verses before the preacher does.
You know when to say "Amen."
You know how to sound strong when someone asks about your faith.
But there are questions you have never dared to ask out loud.
What if I misunderstood something?
What if I have been believing only because my family believed?
What if someone asks me a difficult question about the Bible and I cannot answer?
What if my faith is not as strong as everyone thinks?
And perhaps the most frightening question of all:
What if asking these things means I am failing God?
But look at Luke.
He does not tell Theophilus to stop thinking.
He does not say, "You have already been instructed, so investigation is unnecessary."
He writes an entire Gospel so his reader can understand more securely what he has received.
That does not mean every doubt will disappear.
It does not mean historical research can answer every spiritual or philosophical question.
And it certainly does not mean that faith is nothing more than an academic exercise.
But it does mean that thoughtful investigation is not automatically the enemy of Christian belief.
The God who calls us to love Him with all our heart also calls us to love Him with all our mind (Luke 10:27).
And Luke's next phrase deserves careful attention.
παρηκολουθηκότι ἄνωθεν πᾶσιν ἀκριβῶς
The words describe Luke as having followed or investigated everything carefully from the beginning.
The term akribōs carries the sense of accuracy or careful attention.
The word anōthen can mean "from the beginning" in this context.
Luke is describing the thoroughness of his approach.
He then says he intends to write:
καθεξῆς — kathexēs.
"In order" or "in an orderly sequence."
That does not necessarily mean every event is presented in strict chronological order.
An orderly narrative can also arrange material in a meaningful literary or thematic sequence.
And Luke's Gospel does exactly that.

He carefully develops the story of Jesus, from the announcements surrounding His birth through His ministry, His journey toward Jerusalem, His suffering, His resurrection, and His commissioning of His followers.
Luke is not merely stacking isolated miracles together.
He is guiding his reader through a coherent account of who Jesus is and what His coming means.
Then we arrive at the purpose of it all.
ἵνα ἐπιγνῷς ... τὴν ἀσφάλειαν
"So that you may know ... the certainty."
The Greek word asphaleian can convey security, reliability, or certainty.
Luke wants Theophilus to have a firmer grasp of the teaching he has received.
And notice the tenderness hidden inside that purpose.
Luke is not simply trying to win an argument.
He is serving someone who needs assurance.
Perhaps Theophilus faced questions.
Perhaps he wanted greater confidence in what he had been taught.
We do not know his personal circumstances.
But we do know what Luke hoped his writing would accomplish.
He wanted the truth about Jesus to be understood with confidence.
And here is where the opening of Luke's Gospel becomes much more than an interesting discussion about ancient documents.
Because Luke did not write only about how information was preserved.
He wrote about the One at the center of that information.
Jesus Christ.
The Son of God.
The Savior who entered a world full of sin, grief, injustice, religious pride, broken relationships, and people desperate for mercy.
Luke's Gospel is filled with people whose lives were not clean enough to impress the religious crowd.
A sinful woman weeping at Jesus' feet.
A tax collector despised by his neighbors.
A criminal dying beside the crucified Christ.
A younger son who wasted his inheritance and returned home with nothing.
And in each story, the question becomes painfully personal.
What happens when a human life becomes a scandal?
What happens when the worst thing you have done threatens to become the only thing people remember about you?
What happens when your past speaks louder than your prayers?
Some people know exactly what that feels like.
They know what it is to have their name dragged through conversations they were never invited into.
They know what it is to smile in church while carrying a private history of regret.
They know what it is to love Jesus and still struggle with the consequences of yesterday.
And that is why Luke's Gospel matters so deeply.
Not because it offers us permission to pretend sin is harmless.
Not because Jesus ignores repentance.
But because it shows us a Savior who comes to seek and save the lost.
Listen to the words of Jesus in Luke 19:10:
"For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost."
The Greek is unforgettable:
ζητῆσαι καὶ σῶσαι τὸ ἀπολωλός
"To seek and to save the lost."
Zētēsai — to seek.
Sōsai — to save.
To apolōlos — that which is lost.
Jesus did not come merely to admire people who had already found their way.
He came seeking those who were lost.
And if you have ever felt lost in your own life, that is not a small statement.
It is the difference between a religion that tells you to climb your way back to God and the Gospel that announces a Savior who came into the world to rescue sinners.
But His rescue does not leave us unchanged.
Grace is not a decorative covering for a life determined to remain in rebellion.
Jesus calls sinners to repentance.
In Luke 5:32, He says:
"I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance."
The invitation is merciful.
And it is serious.
Come to Him.
Turn from sin.
Trust Him.
Receive His forgiveness.
Follow Him.
Not because repentance purchases His love, but because the grace that saves us also calls us into a transformed life.
And now consider how extraordinary it is that Luke wanted this message carefully recorded.
Think of the people who first encountered Jesus.
Think of the witnesses who carried His teaching forward.
Think of the communities that preserved and transmitted accounts of His ministry.
Think of Luke taking seriously the responsibility of writing an orderly narrative for someone who needed certainty.
And think of the centuries that followed.
People have questioned these writings.
Studied them.
Translated them.
Argued about them.
Compared manuscripts.
Examined their historical setting.
The existence of early testimony does not, by itself, prove every theological claim in the Gospel. Historical investigation and faith involve related but distinct questions.
Yet Luke's opening is powerful precisely because he does not present the Christian message as something that should never be examined.
He places his work in the context of witnesses, transmission, and careful inquiry.
And then he takes us to Jesus.
To the cross.
To the empty tomb.
To the risen Lord who tells His disciples that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be proclaimed in His name to all nations (Luke 24:46–47).
That is where Luke's Gospel ultimately leads.
Not to Luke.
Not to Theophilus.
Not to an ancient literary debate.
To Jesus Christ crucified and risen.
And maybe that is what you needed to remember tonight.
Your faith does not rest on your ability to answer every objection.
Your salvation does not depend on never experiencing uncertainty.
Your hope is not that you have managed to become a flawless Christian.
Your hope is Jesus Christ.
The One who lived without sin.
The One who gave Himself for sinners.
The One who rose from the dead.
The One who calls you to turn from darkness and trust Him.
The One whose grace is greater than the shame you have carried, though never indifferent to the sin from which He calls you away.
And there is something else.
The story of Luke and Theophilus reminds us that helping another person understand the Gospel is a meaningful act of service.
Someone took the time to preserve testimony.
Someone took the time to teach.
Someone took the time to write.
Someone took the time to explain.
Someone cared whether another person understood the truth.
And that same responsibility belongs to Christians today.
Not every believer will write a Gospel.
The apostolic witness to Christ occupies a unique place in the foundation of the church.
But every believer can bear faithful witness to the Gospel already given to us.
A parent can open Scripture with a child.
A friend can answer a difficult question with patience.
A struggling Christian can admit uncertainty and continue seeking understanding.
A believer can share a Scripture-centered article that helps someone reconsider what they thought they knew about Jesus.
Sometimes the person who needs that encouragement is not a stranger.
Sometimes it is your brother.
Your daughter.
Your closest friend.
The person who stopped attending church and never explained why.
The person who still believes in God but feels too ashamed to pray.
And sometimes it is the person looking back at you in the mirror.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to replace the local church.
Not to sell forgiveness.
Not to suggest that spiritual maturity can be purchased.
But to keep pointing people toward Scripture, repentance, grace, discipleship, and the saving work of Jesus Christ.
And if you have been helped by this ministry, there is a meaningful way to participate in its continued work.
It is the opportunity to help make Christ-centered resources available to others.
And we need to be biblically clear about something.
It does not purchase God's favor, earn forgiveness, or make someone more spiritually worthy.
Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing, generous, and free from compulsion.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
Your regular giving to your local church and your responsibilities toward your family should not be neglected.
What matters is that your giving comes from faith, love, wisdom, and a willing heart.
And for those who are able and genuinely want to help sustain this work, the invitation is open.
You are still welcome here.
The Gospel is not behind a paywall.
And there are other meaningful ways to help.
Not a trivia question about Luke.
Not a test of how much Greek you remember.
Something that reaches deeper.
Have you ever been afraid to ask a question about your faith because you thought God would be disappointed in you?
Maybe you were taught that asking questions meant you were becoming rebellious.
Maybe you have been carrying doubts alone.
Maybe you have heard so many confident religious voices that you have become afraid to admit where you still struggle.
If that is you, consider leaving a comment.
You can simply write, "Lord, help me know Your truth."
Or tell us which question about Scripture you have been afraid to ask.
You do not have to disclose anything private. You do not have to pretend you have every answer. And you do not have to perform spiritual confidence for strangers.
A sincere conversation about God's Word can be a beginning.
Because Luke's introduction gives us a beautiful reminder.
Careful questions and genuine faith do not have to be enemies.
But the ultimate invitation of Luke's Gospel is more than intellectual certainty.
It is to encounter the Christ whom Luke proclaims.
The Savior who welcomes repentant sinners.
The Lord who calls us to follow Him.
The risen Jesus whose mercy is not exhausted by the failures of those who turn to Him.
Perhaps you came to this article wondering why so many people had already written about Jesus.
And now you see the deeper significance.
Luke was not embarrassed that testimony preceded his account.
He acknowledged it.
He investigated carefully.
He wrote in an orderly manner.
And he wanted Theophilus to know the reliability of what he had been taught.
But the greatest treasure in Luke's Gospel is not the method by which Luke wrote.
It is the Savior about whom he wrote.
Because Jesus did not come merely to become the subject of another ancient book.
He came to seek and save the lost.
And if your life has become a story of failure, regret, or disgrace, that does not have to be the final chapter.
Come to Christ in repentance and faith.
His grace does not rewrite history by pretending sin never happened.
His grace changes the future by redeeming sinners whom sin could never save.
And maybe that is the line you need to carry into tomorrow:
The world may remember the chapter where you fell, but in Christ, your fall does not have to be where your story ends.
